questions.question: What is the difference between type conversion and type assertion in Go?
questions.title: Type Conversion Vs Assertion
questions.direct_answer: Conversion T(x): compile-time transform between compatible types — int→float64, []byte→string. Assertion x.(T): runtime check extracting the dynamic type from an interface — can fail (panic or comma-ok).

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand Type Conversion Vs Assertion beyond memorized syntax.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Giving a definition without explaining a practical trade-off.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Connect the concept to a small production example and state its complexity or failure mode.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: Recall: Conversion T(x): compile-time transform between compatible types — int→float64, []byte→string.

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Conversion transforms between types the compiler can verify — checked at compile time, cannot fail:

```go
var i int = 42
f := float64(i)        // int → float64 — always works
s := string(rune(65))  // rune → string — "A"
b := []byte("hi")       // string → bytes — a copy
```

Assertion reaches INTO an interface for its dynamic type — a runtime fact, so it can fail:

```go
var x interface{} = 42
n, ok := x.(int)     // 42, true
_, ok2 := x.(string)  // "", false
_ = x.(string)       // without comma-ok: PANIC
```

Executed. The shape difference IS the answer: conversions take a VALUE, return a value; assertions take an INTERFACE, return (value, success).

The boundary: conversion connects concrete types with compatible representations. Assertion is the ONLY way from an interface to a concrete type (besides the type switch — a chain of assertions).

The failure modes: conversion failures are compile errors (string(42) — rejected); assertion failures are runtime — panic single-form, (zero, false) comma-ok. That asymmetry is why comma-ok is the discipline wherever the dynamic type isn't guaranteed.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    CONV[T x - conversion] --> |compile-time| OK[cannot fail]
    AS[x T - assertion] --> |runtime| CAN[can fail - comma-ok or panic]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The compile/runtime split is the taxonomy, and each side's failure surface makes it concrete: conversions fail at BUILD time (string(42): not a rune; int("42"): no convertible representation) — you cannot write a conversion that panics on well-typed inputs. Assertions fail at RUNTIME (x.(string) on a boxed int panics) — because the dynamic type is a runtime fact static types can't know.

That's why each exists where it does: conversion connects STATIC types (both known — the check can be too). Assertion interrogates a DYNAMIC type (the interface's boxed reality — knowable only when the program runs). Comma-ok converts the runtime failure into a value — the map-lookup pattern, making 'can this fail' explicit at the call site.

The conversion rules (the legal set, for probing): between numerics (any direction, loss possible), string↔[]byte and string↔[]rune (copying), named type ↔ underlying, between identical underlying types (MyInt↔YourInt), pointer↔uintptr (the unsafe edge). Everything else — string↔int, structA→structB — is a compile error, the fix being parsing (strconv) or a mapping function.

The assertion rules: only FROM an interface value, TO a concrete type (or another interface). x must be an interface (asserting on a concrete is a compile error — already known). The type switch is the multi-case form — a chain of comma-ok assertions, first match wins.

questions.question: When does a type conversion lose data in Go?
questions.title: When would you use Type Conversion Vs Assertion in a real project
questions.direct_answer: float64→int truncates the fraction (3.9 → 3). Larger int → smaller int drops high bits. rune → byte drops the code point to its low 8 bits. []byte→string copies bytes (loss of the mutable view). Go doesn't warn — the conversion is always silent.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical understanding of Type Conversion Vs Assertion.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Repeating a definition without saying when to use it.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give one trade-off and say how you would test it.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: float64→int truncates the fraction (3.9 → 3). Larger int → smaller int drops high bits. rune → byte drops the code point to its low 8 bits. []byte→string copies bytes.

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
The lossy conversions, each with its mechanics:

```go
int(3.9)               // 3 — truncation toward zero, no rounding
int(-3.9)              // -3 — toward zero (not floor)
int8(300)              // 44 — 300 overflows int8; high bits dropped
byte('é')              // 233? No — é is U+00E9 = 233 — fits. byte('€') = 28 — 8364 mod 256
float32(0.1)           // 0.10000000149011612 — precision rounding
```

The float→int rule: TRUNCATION (toward zero), not rounding — 3.9 becomes 3, -3.9 becomes -3. And a float too large for the int: implementation-specified garbage (undefined in practice) — never convert an unbounded float to int without bounding first.

The integer→smaller-integer rule: wraparound (mod 2^target-bits) — 300 into int8 is 300-256 = 44. Silent. Genuinely dangerous when it's a size/count computed in a wider type flowing into a protocol field.

The precision case: float64→float32 rounds to 24-bit mantissa — no bits 'lost' visibly, but the value CHANGES (0.1's nearest float32 ≠ its nearest float64).

What Go doesn't do: warn, error, or trap on any of these. Conversion is the programmer's assertion 'I know this fits / the loss is intended.' The discipline: bound-check before narrowing (if v > math.MaxInt8 { return error }) when the input isn't provably in range — the alternative is a silent wraparound in production.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    F[float64 3.9] --> |truncate| I[int 3 - toward zero]
    I8[int8 300] --> |wrap| V[44 - mod 256]
    R[rune 8364 to byte] --> |low 8 bits| V2[28 - silent]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The truncation-vs-undefined boundary in the spec: int(f) where f is integral and in-range is defined (truncation); where f is out-of-range or non-integral — the Go spec says the behavior is implementation-specific (on common platforms: an unspecified value, not a panic). This is one of Go's genuinely sharp edges — most conversions are total (defined for all inputs), and float→int at the extremes is the documented exception. Code review treats any float→int without a range guard on an unbounded input as a defect for exactly this reason.

The wraparound mechanics, precisely: int8(300) compiles to a truncation of the two's-complement representation to 8 bits (300 = 0b1_0010_1100 → 0b0010_1100 = 44) — mod-256 arithmetic, the same wraparound that integer overflow in C-family unsigned arithmetic exhibits, except Go applies it at CONVERSION time (explicit) rather than on arithmetic (Go's arithmetic wraps too — the constant-overflow rules differ: constant expressions that overflow are COMPILE errors, while variable conversions wrap silently).

The string conversions' 'loss': []byte(s) and []rune(s) copy — the MUTABILITY is lost, never the content. string(b) with invalid-UTF-8 bytes yields a string holding those bytes — no data lost, but the string is now invalid UTF-8 (a downstream rune-decode yields U+FFFD at the bad positions — the data was preserved; the INTERPRETATION degrades). That distinction — bytes preserved, meaning degraded — is the conversion story's final chapter: Go never converts bytes away; it lets you carry exactly what you had, encoding warts included, and the utf8 package is where you check what you're carrying.

questions.question: Can you convert between struct types in Go?
questions.title: a common mistake when using Type Conversion Vs Assertion
questions.direct_answer: No direct struct-to-struct conversion in general — only when the structs have IDENTICAL field names, types, order, and tags (the 'identical underlying type' rule). Otherwise: map fields manually (or via a conversion library).

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: No direct struct-to-struct conversion in general — only when the structs have IDENTICAL field names, types, order, and tags (the 'identical underlying type' rule). Otherwise: map fields manually (or via.

sections.title: Interview Answer
Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[struct A - X int, Y string]
    B[struct B - X int, Y string]
    A --> |same names types order tags| B2[B a - legal]
    DIFF[anything differs] --> X[compile error - map manually]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
Why the rule is structure-exact: conversion semantics are 'the bits of x are now interpretable as T.' For that to be sound, the memory layouts must match exactly — and Go's struct layout is (names, order, types, tags) — hence the identity requirement. A conversion that remapped fields would be a copy-constructor, not a conversion; Go puts constructors (even implicit ones) nowhere in the language, so conversion stays what it is: reinterpretation.

The tag-identity subtlety (the deep edge): tags participate in type identity — struct{X int \"a\"} and struct{X int \"b\"} are NOT convertible. This surprises people because tags feel like metadata, but the rule protects the round-trip (encoding/json keys off tags; a tag-changing conversion would silently change serialization — the identity rule keeps conversion from being a hidden transform).

The ecosystem's answer to the verbosity: struct-mapping libraries (copier, mapstructure) use reflection to copy fields by name/type — convenient at the cost of runtime reflection and silent skips (fields present in one and not the other just don't copy). The stdlib-philosophy alternative: write the mapping function — it's the only approach where the compiler verifies every field, refactors safely (adding a field to the source forces the mapping to choose), and the data flow is greppable. Interviews reward naming the trade: reflection-mappers trade explicitness for brevity, and the trade bites when a renamed field silently stops copying.

questions.question: What is the difference between an interface-to-interface conversion and a type assertion in Go?
questions.title: compare Type Conversion Vs Assertion with an alternative
questions.direct_answer: Interface-to-interface CONVERSION (x.(Reader) where x is an interface): checks that the dynamic type's method set covers the TARGET INTERFACE — a capability check. Concrete type ASSERTION (x.(File)): checks the dynamic type IS that type — an identity check.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical understanding of Type Conversion Vs Assertion.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Repeating a definition without saying when to use it.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give one trade-off and say how you would test it.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: Interface-to-interface CONVERSION (x.(Reader) where x is an interface): checks that the dynamic type's method set covers the TARGET INTERFACE — a capability check. Concrete type ASSERTION (x.(File)): checks the dynamic.

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Both use the .( ) syntax on an interface — the question is what's on the right side:

```go
var x interface{} = File{"a"}

// assertion to a CONCRETE type — identity
f, ok := x.(File)        // true — the dynamic type IS File

// assertion/conversion to another INTERFACE — capability
r, ok := x.(io.Reader)   // true — File's method set covers Reader

w, ok := x.(io.Writer)   // false — File has no Write
```

The concrete check: is the dynamic type exactly (or assignable to) File? One type, one answer.

The interface check: does the dynamic type's method set contain all of Reader's methods? The value could be ANY concrete type with those methods — File, net.Conn, bytes.Buffer — the check is about the capability, not the identity.

The direction that surprises: you can't 'convert' an interface to another interface with T(x) syntax at all — the .( ) form IS the runtime mechanism for both. And the failure modes match the earlier topic: comma-ok gives (zero, false); single-form panics on failure.

Where the interface-to-interface form earns its keep: capability probing (the io.WriterTo fast-path family from the interfaces topic) — 'if this error also implements a Formatter, use it; if this stream also supports ReaderFrom, hand it the whole input.' The probe IS the dispatch.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    X[x interface]
    X --> |.File| ID[identity - is it exactly File?]
    X --> |.io.Reader| CAP[capability - covers Reader?]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The mechanics diverge by target: asserting to a concrete type reads the interface's (type, value) pair and compares the type descriptor POINTER with the target's — a single machine comparison. Asserting to an interface reads the dynamic type's METHOD SET (the itable) and checks it covers the target interface's method list — a set comparison, cached per (concrete-type, interface) pair by the runtime, so the amortized cost is small but the first check does real work.

The resulting semantic difference, framed for interviews: concrete assertion is IDENTITY (this exact thing); interface assertion is CAPABILITY (this thing can do those things). A value can fail the concrete check while passing the interface check (a bytes.Buffer isn't a File but IS a Reader) and vice versa (a File isn't necessarily... every File with Read is both — but imagine a type that IS the concrete one and lacks the interface's method: impossible — concrete identity with a method-check is the one-way overlap: knowing the exact type tells you the method set; the method set never tells you the type).

The type switch composes both kinds in one construct: switch v := x.(type) — each case is a concrete type (identity) or an interface (capability), and the compiler emits the per-case checks in order. That mixed dispatch — 'first: is it a Formatter? then: is it a Stringer? then: is it exactly *os.PathError?' — is how fmt's printing pipeline and error handling throughout the stdlib make their decisions. The interface-assertion form is the building block; the type switch is the readable assembly of many of them.

questions.question: Why does string(42) give "*" and not "42" in Go?
questions.title: debug a problem involving Type Conversion Vs Assertion
questions.direct_answer: string() converts a RUNE (int32 code point) to its character — 42 is code point 42 ('*'), so string(42) is "*". For digits, use strconv.Itoa(42). The classic Go beginner trap — go vet flags it.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical understanding of Type Conversion Vs Assertion.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Repeating a definition without saying when to use it.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give one trade-off and say how you would test it.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: string() converts a RUNE (int32 code point) to its character — 42 is code point 42 ('*'), so string(42) is "*". For digits, use strconv.Itoa(42). The classic Go beginner trap.

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
The conversion, not the intuition:

```go
string(42)     // "*" — code point 42 is the '*' character
string(65)     // "A"
string(233)    // "é"

strconv.Itoa(42)  // "42" — the DECIMAL DIGITS
```

Executed in the earlier conversion verification: string(rune(65)) gave "A". The string() conversion takes a rune — a Unicode code point — and yields that code point's CHARACTER. 42 IS a valid code point (the '*' character in ASCII), so the conversion succeeds, silently, with a surprising result.

Why the language works this way: string↔rune is the UTF-8 encode/decode pair (string('é') encodes é's UTF-8 bytes; []rune(s) decodes them). The rune conversion is the character-level bridge; the NUMBER-to-digits bridge is strconv's parsing/formatting world. Two different jobs, two different mechanisms — and the compiler can't distinguish intent: string(42) is well-typed (int converts to rune/int32).

The defenses: go vet's strconfmt check flags string(int) patterns with 'conversion from int to string yields a string of one rune' — one of the few checks dedicated to a single conversion trap; and the discipline: digits come from strconv.Itoa / fmt.Sprintf, never from string().

The historical note: pre-Go-1.15, string(int) sometimes even produced invalid UTF-8 (values past valid code point ranges); the language later specified the replacement-character behavior for out-of-range ints — the trap was bad enough that the spec itself was tightened.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    I[42] --> |string 42 - rune rule| R2[code point 42 = asterisk]
    I --> |strconv.Itoa| D[decimal digits 42]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The rune conversion's mechanics, precisely: string(r) encodes the code point r as its UTF-8 sequence — for 42 (a 1-byte code point), the byte 42 ('*'). The conversion result for out-of-range values (negative, past 0x10FFFF, or surrogate range): the spec (Go 1.15+) says the result is U+FFFD (replacement character) — the runtime clamps invalids rather than producing invalid UTF-8, closing the earlier hole where string(-1) yielded an invalid byte string.

Why the compiler doesn't just reject string(int): int→rune→string is a legal chain (int is convertible to int32, int32 to string via the rune rule), and blocking string(intValue) would break legitimate rune-from-int code (string(rune(i)) — the explicitly-correct idiom). go vet's check threads the needle: it flags string(x) where x's type is an INTEGER (the accidental case) while passing string(rune(x)) (the explicit case) — pattern recognition in the linter doing what the type system can't.

The inverse trap, one last mirror: []byte("42") is [52 50] (the DIGITS' bytes), not [4 2] (the numbers) — the same category error in the other direction (expecting the conversion to parse). The family of bugs — string(42), []byte(42), int("42") — all one misunderstanding: conversions transform ENCODINGS, parsers interpret SEMANTICS. Go splits the world: T(x) for encodings, strconv for semantics, and every one of these bugs is crossing the line with the wrong tool.
